worksheet.title: Which One Is Wrong?
worksheet.subtitle: One script misses the goal — find it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can compare two scripts to a goal and find which one has a bug.

parts.title: The goal: meet on 3
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag. They are SUPPOSED to MEET on number 3. But one of the two scripts has a bug, so it does not reach 3. Read both scripts, run them, and figure out WHICH sprite's script is wrong.

parts.title: Run both
parts.prompt: Where does each land? Bit (home 0, forward 3): ____  Pixel (home 5, back 1): ____. Do BOTH reach the goal 3?

parts.title: Which one is wrong?
parts.prompt: Which sprite's script is WRONG — Bit's or Pixel's? Write it. How do you know? (Hint: one sprite already reaches 3.)

parts.title: How far off?
parts.prompt: The goal is 3. The wrong sprite landed on ____. That is ____ number(s) away from the goal.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To find a bug in two scripts, compare each one to the GOAL. The script that already reaches the goal is correct. The one that misses is the buggy one — and that tells you where to look.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Debugging & Reading Code
teacher_guide.title: Which One Is Wrong?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. Which One Is Wrong? — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students learn the key debugging move: compare EACH set of moves to the goal to find the bug. The goal is to meet on 3; Bit reaches it and Pixel does not, so Pixel's set is the buggy one. Find which is wrong before fixing it. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel) so children can trace both sets of moves and see which one misses the goal.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Check each character against the goal: the one that misses has the bug.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit reaches 3, Pixel lands on 4.
3. Let them try. Students name the buggy set and find how far off it is (Ex 2–3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Bit: 0, forward 3 → 3. Pixel: 5, back 1 → 4. Bit reaches the goal 3; Pixel does not.
Exercise 2 — Pixel's set is wrong; we know because Bit already lands on the goal, so the bug is in the other set.
Exercise 3 — the goal is 3; Pixel landed on 4, which is 1 number away. (This sheet only LOCATES the bug; fixing comes next.)

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: assuming both are wrong. Only the one that misses the goal has the bug.
Make it easier: mark the goal on the line and see which counter does not land there.
Make it harder: ask how they know it is Pixel and not Bit.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions, including two sets that run at the same time.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read two sets of instructions, find and fix the wrong one, and explain the fix.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child names the buggy set and says how far off the goal it landed.
